text: The last eight each fit in a single cell. Sum if adds the values that meet one condition, and sum ifs several. North sums to five sixty, and North in March to two ninety. Count if and count ifs count them instead: three North orders are over a hundred. Average if does means, and North averages one forty. Trim strips the extra spaces, and proper fixes the case: the messy name comes back as Ava Smith. Clean before you look up, or the keys won't match. Left with find splits at a character: everything before the at sign is the username. Text join puts the pieces back, and skips the blanks. A date is stored as a serial number of days. March first, twenty twenty-four, is forty-five thousand three hundred fifty-two, so March thirty-first minus March first is thirty. A date stored as text won't sort or subtract until date value converts it. Conditional formatting colors cells by a rule. Over a hundred fifty, and two orders light up. Use it to scan, not instead of a chart. A named range gives a cell a name, so A two times tax rate reads as what it means, and still points at F one. And to find duplicates, count each value against its own column: a count over one flags the repeated email. Check the flags, then remove duplicates. A good table answers the question. A good chart gets someone to believe it. Next: data visualization.
